To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) perceptual differences in place of articulation are consistent across four language communities; (ii) perceptual salience scales of place of articuation for released stops are consistent with cross-linguistically common major place assimilation patterns; and (iii) the perceptual salience of unreleased stops does not follow the same pattern.

the perceptual salience of places of articulation was affected by the presence or absence of releases in the stop consonants, and that the perceptual differences in salience between places of articulations corresponded to cross linguistic patterns of assimilation for the released stop consonants, but not for the unreleased ones.
(a) the perceptual salience of stops is affected by release, and that (b) the salience scale is not identical for released and unreleased stops.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of phonetics in phonology and the relationship between the two.
the relation between phonetics and phonology, and with the nature of phonological markedness.
the question of how phonological categories are grounded in the perceptual system and how they are acquired.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
phonetic knowledge is a necessary, but not a sufficient, condition for explaining phonological patterns.
phonetic knowledge is not a sufficient predictor of patterns of phonological assimilation.
the phonological patterns of place assimilation are not fully predictable on the basis of perceptual saliency alone, and that other factors are also involved.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the phonetic knowledge hypothesis can explain some of the crosslinguistic phonological patterns, but not all of them.

the phonetic grounding of the phonological system is not as direct as it was once thought, and the phonetic knowledge hypothesis is only a partial explanation for the relation between phonetic difficulty and assimilation.
phonetic difficulty is a major factor in phonological markedness, but it is not the only factor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
phonetic grounding of phonological patterns is a complex process that involves both perceptual and production mechanisms, and is affected by language-specific factors.
the perceptibility of stops in a language is affected by the presence or absence of a release.

phonological processes can be predicted from phonetic knowledge, but only when phonetic knowledge is measured in terms of perceptibility of phonetic features, rather than in terms of articulatory difficulty.
